introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoke of Muḥammad in the churches and synagogues of Europe and America, where, he says, the Prophet’s name had been mentioned only with contempt. These eighty-eight passages give his argument and the testimony of Bahá’u’lláh and the Báb: judge the Prophet by what he did, a people raised from tribal war to a civilization that taught Europe; read the Qur’an; and let a thousand years of enmity between Christians and Muslims end. The guide is given whole. Beside it stand eighty-eight voices from elsewhere, many of them the verses of the Qur’an that the readings quote or lean on, with the Bible’s nearest parallels, and a few Western writers who broke with the old contempt or kept it: Carlyle, Locke, Dante, Boccaccio. Most stand close to the reading they follow. About one in six asks something harder, about the sword, about civilization as a proof, about finality, and those end in a question.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sets aside the traditions for and against Muḥammad and looks at what he brought about. What would it mean to judge any religious founder that way, and what would it leave out?
The rise of Arab civilization is offered as the greatest proof of his prophethood. Jesus said his kingdom was not of this world. How far can worldly results count as evidence in religion?

The readings say war was sanctioned to protect the community; the Qur’an says “begin not hostilities” and “no compulsion in religion”; Jesus said to turn the other cheek. How do you understand the difference between these teachings?
Carlyle defended Muḥammad and found the Qur’an “toilsome reading”. What has your own experience been of reading the scripture of a faith not your own, and what helped?
Muḥammad is called the Seal of the Prophets, and Hebrews says God has spoken “in these last days” by his Son. How do the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh, in these readings, speak of that finality?

A thousand years of enmity are put down to “misunderstanding and spiritual blindness”. Which misunderstandings between Christians and Muslims do you meet today, and what in these readings answers them?

outside.why: “Read it, that haply ye may find the Truth, for this Book is verily the Straight Path.” The Qur’an’s opening chapter, said in every Muslim prayer, asks to be shown that path.

Bahá’u’lláh tells Christians to read the Qur’an. Carlyle, who defended Muḥammad to a London audience, found the book itself “as toilsome reading as I ever undertook”. What does a reader need in order to read another people’s scripture well?

A thousand years of enmity between Muslims and Christians, “owing to misunderstanding and spiritual blindness”. Carlyle said so in 1840: the lies heaped round this man are disgraceful to ourselves only.

If prejudices were abandoned, “there would be no enmity whatever between them”. Boccaccio’s wise Jew, asked by Saladin which of the three laws is true, tells of three rings no one can tell apart. Is peace between the religions reached by leaving the question open, or by answering it?
The tablet addresses the Prophet with this verse: “We sent thee not save as a mercy to the worlds.”
“We believe in all the Prophets, making no distinction between any of His Messengers.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is quoting the Qur’an’s own creed.
“Our faith is real … it is based on investigation, not blind imitation.” The Qur’an’s reproach to those who say: we follow that wherein we found our fathers.
There are Bahá’ís who “subscribe to the truth of Islam”. Locke had asked far less of Christian Europe, and was thought bold: that no Muslim be shut out from civil rights for his religion.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoke of Muḥammad in churches and synagogues. Paul began in Athens with what his hearers already honoured: whom ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
“It was impossible to mention His name in churches and temples.” Jesus on how prophets are received: a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country.

In the West no good was spoken of the Prophet. Dante, who shared the contempt, still set Avicenna and Averroes among the great minds of antiquity. What does it mean to honour a civilization’s scholars and despise its founder?
“We do not consider diverse traditions, either for him or against him. We consider what has been shown forth by him.” Jesus’ own test: by their fruits ye shall know them.
Muḥammad brought “the warring, hostile, and savage tribes” under one pavilion. The Qur’an reminds them: ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts, so that ye became as brothers.
A divine educator is needed to turn enmity into fellowship. The Qur’an says no wealth could have done it: thou couldst not have attuned their hearts, but God hath attuned them.
He “taught them to look upon each other as brothers”. Paul says the same of what Christ did between Jew and Gentile: he hath broken down the middle wall of partition.
“He educated these barbarous tribes.” The Prophet’s own account of his mission, as Málik reports it.

The Muslim refugees tell the king of Abyssinia: we were idolaters, and God sent us a prophet. Paul’s converts are described in the same words: ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
“We worshipped many gods … we practiced many evil deeds.” Muslims call that age the time of ignorance; Paul used the same phrase at Athens.
The rise of this people “in such a short interval” is called the greatest proof of his prophethood. Carlyle saw the same fact: a spark on black sand, and the sand blazes from Delhi to Grenada.
Arab science, government and arts are the demonstration offered. Jesus told Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world. Is the civilization a religion builds a proof of its truth?
Ignorant peoples became “the foremost among the learned in all sciences and arts”. The first word revealed to Muḥammad, by tradition, was a command to read.
Baghdad became the centre of learning. The Qur’an’s question behind it: are those who know equal with those who know not?
For thirteen years he suffered; then an army came to exterminate his followers. This verse is the first permission to resist: sanction is given unto those who fight because they have been wronged.
“Muhammad never fought against the Christians; on the contrary, He treated them with consideration.” The Qur’an on Christians: the nearest in affection to those who believe.
The Christians of Najrán were given freedom. The Qur’an’s invitation to them: come to an agreement between us and you, that we shall worship none but God.
“When the Light of Muhammad shone forth all Arabia was brightened.” Isaiah: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
“These oppressed and degraded peoples became enlightened.” Mary’s song: he hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
“Mohammed through his power was enabled to elevate a nation.” Machiavelli would have said why: armed prophets conquer and unarmed ones are destroyed. Was it by arms that the nation was elevated?
“Europe’s current advancement was in reality derived from Arab Spain.” Kipling’s ballad allows that East and West do meet, and on what terms.

Europeans attended the schools of Andalusia and carried the sciences home. The Preacher: is there any thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? How much of what any civilization calls its own was learned from another?
The Muḥammadan light “established the foundation of divine justice”. Amos: let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
With what power did he reform “primitive, savage Arabs” into a people? Paul on how God chooses: the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
God raised him up among tribes “fallen to the depths of ignorance and blindness”. Ezekiel’s valley of dry bones: come, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.
“A valley without farms, where nothing would grow.” Abraham’s prayer in the Qur’an over the same valley: I have settled some of my posterity in an uncultivable valley near Thy holy House.
“So savage that fathers would bury their daughters alive.” The Qur’an puts the question to the child herself on the last day: for what sin she was slain.
Muḥammad “was unlettered and held no intercourse with nations”. The Qur’an: He hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own.
A man without learning who taught a people. The same was said of Jesus: how knoweth this man letters, having never learned?
He “knew not the laws”. The Qur’an makes it an argument: thou wast not a reader of any scripture before it, nor didst thou write it.
“Tonight is the night of the birth of the Prophet.” Luke’s account of another birth night, kept by another third of mankind.
Mecca, “a rocky tract — no trees, no vegetation”, became the place to which Asia and Africa turn. Isaiah: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
The Arabian desert “became the mother of all the countries”. Genesis records a promise about Abraham’s other son: as for Ishmael, I will make him a great nation.
The wilderness of sand became the Ka‘ba of millions. Muslim readers have long heard Arabia in Moses’ blessing: he shined forth from mount Paran.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that powerful nations now justify intervention abroad as a duty of the civilized, and yet object when the Prophet did the like. Kipling gave that duty its name in 1899. What separates civilizing a people from conquering them?
“He sanctioned war for the preservation of the lives of His followers.” The limits as the Qur’an states them: fight those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities.
There must be a law “to prevent the wolves from destroying the lambs”. Augustine to a Christian general: war should be waged only as a necessity.

Muḥammad gave the law of the community’s justice and allowed the sword in defence. Jesus: resist not evil; whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. Are these two laws for two kinds of time, or two answers to one question?
The talk says he commanded his followers to carry the religion by the sword. The Qur’an says: there is no compulsion in religion. How should the two statements be read together?
“Thou didst conquer Thy cities … with spears and swords.” Moses’ song at the Red Sea speaks as plainly: the Lord is a man of war.
Hearts were united, and lands taken by the sword. Even Jesus, on his last night, said: he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one. What place have the scriptures left for force?
When his sons died, the idolaters called him “cut off”. This short chapter of the Qur’an is the answer given him.
A prophet mocked for leaving no son. Isaiah’s promise to the childless who keep faith: a name better than of sons and of daughters.
“Whenever tribulation and adversity touched him in the path of God, he remained patient.” The Prophet, asked who is tried most severely: the prophets, then those nearest to them.
A hundred thousand were counted companions; “those who acted upon His teachings and were God-fearing were found to be few”. Jesus: many are called, but few are chosen.
Many had associated with him; few followed. Jesus healed ten lepers and one came back: where are the nine?
At his death the Prophet asked for paper, and the community that followed disagreed about what he would have written. Paul saw parties form in his own lifetime: I am of Paul; and I of Apollos.
“A proper history was never written in Islam.” Luke explains why he wrote his: many have taken in hand to set forth a declaration, and it seemed good to me also to write in order.
Bahá’u’lláh’s writings share a natural philosophy with “the Persian Sufis”. Rúmí’s lines on the soul’s passage through mineral, plant, animal and man are its best-known statement.
“Originally we were Mohammedan, but since the declaration of Bahá’u’lláh we love all humanity.” A Muslim mystic six centuries earlier: my heart has become capable of every form.
Muslims thought Muḥammad the greater for his title. The Qur’an itself says of the messengers that some excel others, and names Jesus among those exalted.
In the time of Jesus “spirituality and spiritual life was far greater”. Jesus ranks John the Baptist above all born of women and below the least in the kingdom. What are such rankings for?
Rúmí’s Masnaví was “like unto a column erected to buttress a tilting wall”. The poem begins with a reed flute lamenting its separation from the reed-bed.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes this answer of the Prophet: am I aught save a mortal messenger?
And this: had I knowledge of the unseen, I should have abundance of wealth.
A messenger who insists he is mortal. Paul and Barnabas, taken for gods at Lystra: we also are men of like passions with you.
Seven tribes made their faith conditional on a miracle. Jesus met the same demand: there shall no sign be given, but the sign of the prophet Jonas.
Each asked for a wonder. Jesus: except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.
The Qur’an refuses to rest the Prophet’s claim on miracles. Hume argued that no testimony is sufficient to establish one. Do the scripture and the sceptic agree here, and on what?
The verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites: Jews, Christians and Sabaeans, whoever believes and does right, no fear shall come upon them.
The Báb appeared twelve hundred and seventy years after Muḥammad, with proofs. Jesus had said there was more to come: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
God caused Islam to endure, and then sent another. Jesus on what a new revelation does to the old: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
God “sealed the Messengers with Muhammad”. The verse from which the title comes.

In every age a Prophet and a Book, until the seal. Hebrews also speaks of a last word: God hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. How do the Bahá’í writings read claims of finality in earlier scriptures?
This is the Day which the Seal of the Prophets “gave unto all as a glad-tiding”. In the Qur’an Jesus too brings good tidings of one to come after him.
Muḥammad “is more submissive than anyone possessing submission and more humble than anyone possessing humility”. The same is said of Moses: very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth.
The Báb bears witness and calls down blessings on him. The verse that asks every believer to do so.
The Báb’s testimony quotes this verse: vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth all vision.
God made him “unique among all peers and equals”. Carlyle’s portrait, from outside the faith: a silent great soul, one of those who cannot but be in earnest.
He is the One who “raised up Muhammad and made Him a Messenger to all the worlds”. Moses’ promise, which Muslims read of him: a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee.
His grace “caused dust to ascend above the heavens”. The Psalm: he raiseth up the poor out of the dust, that he may set him with princes.
“The pebbles in his hand bore witness.” Jesus, told to silence his disciples: if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
The dust proclaimed and the trees spoke. Isaiah: the mountains shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
Through his companions “the lands were conquered”. The Qur’an tells him what to do in the hour of triumph: hymn the praises of thy Lord, and seek forgiveness of Him.

“Through them God conquered the world.” Tertullian, in the first Christian centuries, wanted nothing to do with worldly learning or power. Is conquest a strange thing to praise in the companions of a prophet?
“Were it not for Thee, I would not have created the celestial spheres.” Paul says of Christ: all things were created by him, and for him.
The Prophet prayed, “Lord, increase my wonderment in Thee.” The Qur’an teaches him a kindred prayer: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
Wonderment sought, not escaped. Socrates: wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
Bahá’ís are to gain “a sound knowledge of the history and tenets of Islam” from unbiased sources. Mill: he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.

The Qur’an should be studied “to some extent”, without the years mastery would take, “unless they really want to”. The Preacher: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh. How much study does understanding another faith require?

quran-no-knowledge-of-the-unseen.text: Say: For myself I have no power to benefit, nor power to hurt, save that which Allah willeth. Had I knowledge of the Unseen, I should have abundance of wealth, and adversity would not touch me. I am but a warner, and a bearer of good tidings unto folk who believe.

quran-sanction-to-fight.text: Sanction is given unto those who fight because they have been wronged; and Allah is indeed Able to give them victory;

quran-messenger-among-the-unlettered.text: He it is Who hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own, to recite unto them His revelations and to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom, though heretofore they were indeed in error manifest,

quran-not-a-reader-before-it.text: And thou (O Muhammad) wast not a reader of any scripture before it, nor didst thou write it with thy right hand, for then might those have doubted, who follow falsehood.

quran-word-common-between-us.text: Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you: that we shall worship none but Allah, and that we shall ascribe no partner unto Him, and that none of us shall take others for lords beside Allah. And if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are they who have surrendered (unto Him).

quran-valley-without-cultivation.text: Our Lord! Lo! I have settled some of my posterity in an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House, our Lord! that they may establish proper worship; so incline some hearts of men that they may yearn toward them, and provide Thou them with fruits in order that they may be thankful.

quran-no-strain-in-religion.text: And strive for Allah with the endeavour which is His right. He hath chosen you and hath not laid upon you in religion any hardship; the faith of your father Abraham (is yours). He hath named you Muslims of old time and in this (Scripture), that the messenger may be a witness against you, and that ye may be witnesses against mankind. So establish worship, pay the poor-due, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protecting friend. A blessed Patron and a blessed Helper!

quran-abundance.text: Lo! We have given thee Abundance; So pray unto thy Lord, and sacrifice. Lo! it is thy insulter (and not thou) who is without posterity
